newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean unions backing down, unionist arrested.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean unions backing down, unionist arrested.

text.p: South Korean strike leaders on Saturday abandoned calls for indefinite stoppages in protest against a controversial labour law and said they would limit their industrial action.
Police arrested a shipyard unionist, bringing to five the the number of union leaders picked up since South Korean courts last week issued warrants for the arrest of 20 labour leaders.

In a sign union bosses were wilting under government pressure, the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said strikes would be held each Wednesday but warned of an "all-out struggle" from February 18 unless the labour law was dumped.

"From next week, full strikes will take place only on Wednesday. On other week days, union members will work normally," Kwon Young-kil, president of the outlawed confederation, told a news conference.
"Every Saturday we will hold protest rallies after work."
Police arrested Kim Il-shik, confederation leader of Hyundai Heavy Industries, the country's largest shipyard, in an early morning raid in the southeast city of Ulsan.
"Hyundai Heavy union leader Kim Il-shik was arrested this morning in an apartment," a police official said by telephone.
Police said Kim was charged with obstructing business.

Kwon and six deputies, who have led more than three weeks of stoppages in protest at the law which allows firms to dismiss workers and replace strikers, are sheltering from arrest at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.

Earlier this week four union officials from Halla Heavy Industries were arrested, also on charges of obstructing business. State prosecutors have warned the strike leaders they faced arrest unless they dropped industrial action immediately.
The Labour Ministry said the strikes had tapered off. It said around 30,000 workers were now on strike.
Highlighting that only pockets of resistance remain, Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, the nation's largest carmaker, reopened on Saturday after a week of temporary shutdowns.
The government of President Kim Young-sam has refused to revise or revoke the law, arguing labour reform is crucial to trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.
It has heaped pressure on the seven confederation fugitives, slipping a tight security noose around the cathedral.
Special forces officers trained in unarmed combat guarded approaches to the church on Saturday and checked passing cars in an apparent bid to stop union activists slipping in or out.
Kwon denied a report by the state-run Korea Broadcasting System which said the confederation would halt strikes completely if the implementation of the law was delayed.
A spokesman called Kwon's comments at the news conference a "change of tactics" aimed at prolonging protests against the law.
South Korea's Roman Catholic Cardinal Stephen Kim, who met President Kim on Friday, has appealed to both sides to end the crisis through dialogue.
On Friday, the ruling New Korea Party scorned Kwon's acceptance of an offer for a televised debate over the law, saying it could not guarantee the safety of a wanted man.
Kwon was taking up party chairman Lee Hong-koo's suggestion for a televised, round-table discussion between the ruling party leaders and unspecified union heads.
The New Korea Party called on unions to put forward more suitable candidates to debate the law, passed in a dawn sitting of parliament on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
